title: The role of receptive arts and culture to improve anxiety, depression and psychological distress in young people: A realist review
description:
Background: Arts and culture are increasingly recognised as potential supports for mental health, yet little distinction has been made between receptive engagement (e.g. visiting museums, watching performances, listening to music) and active participation (e.g. creating art or attending classes). There is limited understanding of how, for whom, and under what circumstances receptive engagement may influence anxiety, depression, and psychological distress in young people.
Method: We conducted a realist review of evidence up to February 2026 to examine how receptive arts and cultural engagement may affect mental health in young people aged 16–24 years. An initial programme theory, developed through the Online Active Community Engagement programme, stakeholder consultation, and peer research, informed the search and guided analysis. We searched five academic databases and relevant grey literature. Eligible documents were screened against predefined criteria. Context–mechanism–outcome configurations (CMOCs) were developed iteratively with peer researchers and the research team to refine the programme theory.
Results: Eleven documents were included. Evidence supported CMOCs indicating that receptive engagement may support mental health through: (i) short-term affective relief via attentional shift and escapism; (ii) reflection and perspective-taking through exposure to diverse viewpoints; (iii) increased belonging through perceived human connection; (iv) identity safety through representation and inclusive content; and (v) support for emotion regulation when engagement is regular and accessible. Effects were most consistent for proximal outcomes during or shortly after engagement, with limited evidence for sustained reductions in anxiety, depression, or psychological distress beyond the engagement period.

title: EcoTherapistVR: Design and Proof-of-Concept Implementation of a Decentralized Blockchain-Based Virtual Reality Platform for Mental Health Nature Therapy
description: Nature therapy has demonstrated significant benefits for mental health conditions including depression, anxiety, PTSD, and stress-related disorders. However, accessibility barriers prevent many individuals from experiencing natural environments due to physical disabilities, geographic limitations, hospitalization, or financial constraints. Virtual Reality technology offers immersive nature experiences that produce physiological responses similar to actual nature exposure, yet current platforms operate on centralized models with limited content diversity, opaque provenance tracking, and insufficient creator compensation mechanisms. This research presents the design and proof-of-concept implementation of EcoTherapistVR, a blockchain-enabled decentralized platform that delivers immersive VR nature therapy experiences while ensuring content transparency, automated creator compensation, and user privacy. Authors developed a prototype platform utilizing Ethereum blockchain for content tokenization, InterPlanetary File System (IPFS) for decentralized storage, and Unity3D for VR environment rendering. High-resolution 360-degree nature footage was captured from five distinct locations (waterfalls, forests, mountains, beaches, and meadows). Smart contracts manage content ownership, access rights, and automated creator compensation. The system was validated through technical performance testing and user experience evaluation with 40 participants using the System Usability Scale (SUS). The proof-of-concept demonstrates technical feasibility with measured blockchain transaction latency of 2.3 seconds (±0.4s), IPFS content retrieval time of 1.8 seconds (±0.3s) for 4K video initialization, and VR environment loading within 1.8 seconds. User experience testing yielded a mean SUS score of 94.81 (SD=3.12, range 87.5-100), achieving Grade A+ classification. title: Protocol for a systematic review of Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART®) for the treatment of Posttraumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in adults
description:
Introduction
People who suffer from posttraumatic stress disorder (PTSD) often experience intrusion symptoms, negative alterations in cognitions and mood, alterations in arousal and reactivity and avoidance of stimuli associated with the traumatic event. Accordingly, Accelerated Resolution Therapy (ART®) aims to reduce these symptoms. ART® is a brief type of therapy that uses techniques such as rapid eye movement, in vivo exposure, and image rescripting to recondition stressful memories (Kip et al., 2012). Currently only modest support for ART® in the treatment of PTSD has been established using the Chambless and Hollon (1998) criteria for Empirically Supported Treatments (EST). ART® has yet to be re-evaluated using the criteria for determining an EST that were proposed by Tolin et al. (2015). Furthermore, there have been no systematic reviews conducted on the use of ART® for the treatment of PTSD in adults. We aim to address this gap by providing a systematic review of the evidence for ART® in the treatment of PTSD in adults. In addition, an assessment of risk of bias on the outcomes of ART® on PTSD will be conducted. 

Methods and analysis
The Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions (Higgins et al., 2022) will be used to inform the methods of this review. This protocol was developed in accordance with the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analysis Protocols (PRISMA-P; Moher et al., 2015). Search terms were developed in collaboration with a medical librarian. Five electronic peer-reviewed databases, three registers, and three organization websites will be searched. Eligible articles will be independently assessed against inclusion criteria by two reviewers (EM and DS). A quantitative synthesis of findings will be reported where three or more papers with a low risk of bias report on an outcome of interest. title: Personalized Prediction of Momentary Affect with Passive Smartphone Sensing Data in a Clinically Heterogeneous Sample: An evaluation of machine learning and mixed effects approaches
description: Passive smartphone sensing offers a scalable, low-burden approach to continuous mental health monitoring, yet most studies which use passive sensing features to predict momentary psychological states rely on small, clinically homogeneous samples, limiting generalizability and clinical utility. This study compares methods for personalized prediction of momentary affect, stress, and fatigue using passive sensing in a large, clinically diverse sample of 308 adults (66% with a psychiatric diagnosis). Participants completed 15 days of ecological momentary assessment (23,560 total observations) with passive sensing of GPS, accelerometer, phone call, screen-on-time, and sleep data. We predicted five continuous outcomes: positive affect, negative affect, stress, energy, and a depression composite. We explored methods for balancing group-level and personalized prediction, including mixed effects regression tree (MERT) boosting, a method that blends mixed effects and machine learning approaches. We compared this to group-level pooled models, fully personalized models, and linear mixed models. A key finding was that the use of cluster-mean centering (CMC) as a preprocessing step dramatically improved pooled machine learning model performance, enabling a simple XGBoost model to match or exceed fully personalized and MERT boosting approaches. Best models compared favorably to past work predicting continuous momentary affect, achieving overall R-squared of 0.38-0.49 and average idiographic R-squared of 0.16-0.26 calculated on held out test data, with energy and the depression composite emerging as the most predictable outcomes. These results carry direct clinical implications: scalable group-level models can rival personalized models when data are appropriately preprocessed, lowering barriers to real-world deployment of passive sensing–based monitoring. The high predictability of energy and the depressive composite highlights viable targets for just-in-time adaptive interventions

title: Cognitive functioning and Anxiety/Depression: Accounting for Genetic Confounding in the ALSPAC Cohort.
description:
Aims: Depression and anxiety are leading contributors to the global burden of disease, yet the mechanisms underlying these conditions, including the role of cognitive processes, remain uncertain. Cognitive deficits in domains such as emotion recognition, working memory, and response inhibition are commonly observed in individuals with depression and anxiety, but it is unclear whether these reflect causal risk factors, consequences of symptoms, or shared aetiological influences. We investigated whether associations between cognitive function and mental health outcomes persist after accounting for genetic confounding using data from the Avon Longitudinal Study of Parents and Children (ALSPAC).

Methods: Participants completed computer-based assessments of emotion recognition, working memory, and response inhibition at age 24. Depression and anxiety diagnoses were derived at age 24 using the Clinical Interview Schedule - Revised. Logistic regression models examined associations between cognitive function and each mental health outcome, followed by models adjusting for sociodemographic confounders, cognitive confounders, and polygenic scores (PGS) for depression and anxiety. Genetic sensitivity analyses (Gsens) were conducted to estimate the extent to which associations were attributable to shared genetic liability.

Results: Higher working memory performance was consistently associated with lower odds of anxiety, and this association was robust to adjustment for observed confounders and PGS, with Gsens analyses indicating no evidence of genetic confounding. Evidence for an association between working memory and depression was weak and disappeared after accounting for genetic confounding. title: The Role of Intolerance of Uncertainty in Bipolar Disorder
description:
Objectives
Intolerance of Uncertainty (IU) is a dispositional trait arising from negative beliefs about uncertainty. IU has been found to be associated with various psychological disorders, including anxiety and depression, but little is known about its role in bipolar disorder (BD). The present study investigates the presentation of IU in BD, including exploring its relationship with mania and impulsivity. 
Method
Participants with a self-reported diagnosis of BD (n = 93), unipolar depression (n = 90) and control participants (n = 91) were recruited from a participant recruitment platform to complete an online survey. Groups were compared on a variety of measures, including IU, mania symptoms, impulsivity and neuroticism, and a correlation analysis was performed comparing IU to mania and IU to impulsivity. 
Results
BD participants scored more highly than depression participants and controls on all measures except neuroticism, which was found to be equivalent to the depression group. IU positively correlated with mania even when neuroticism was controlled for. IU positively correlated with impulsivity but only in the BD group, and this effect was lost when neuroticism was controlled for. 
Conclusion
This study provides evidence for the importance of IU as a higher-order factor in BD, which extends our understanding of the disorder. Findings could help explain why anxiety is prevalent in BD and provide opportunities for an increase in effectiveness of treatments.

title: Rethinking Personalization in Adolescent Digital Mental Health: Toward Adaptive Behavioral Systems
description:
Digital mental health technologies are increasingly used to support adolescent wellbeing, yet many interventions continue to struggle with long-term engagement and sustainable behavioral impact. A major limitation is that personalization in existing systems often relies on static user profiles, isolated mood reports, or short-term engagement metrics, while adolescent emotional and behavioral needs change continuously across developmental and social contexts.
Current digital mental health interventions remain constrained not simply by limited personalization, but by their inability to adapt to evolving behavioral patterns over time. In response, it proposes Adaptive Behavioral Systems (ABS) as a conceptual framework for digital mental health support that adapts to evolving behavioral trajectories rather than isolated behavioral events.
The framework is organized around six interconnected dimensions: trajectory-based behavioral understanding, iterative adaptation, interpretable behavioral intelligence, integration of behavioral theory, context sensitivity, and autonomy-supportive design. Rather than optimizing engagement alone, Adaptive Behavioral Systems aim to support sustainable self-regulation, coping stability, and behavioral resilience over time.
The paper further examines implications for research, intervention design, ethics, equity, and public policy, particularly in relation to vulnerable adolescent populations affected by social inequality, migration-related stress, and unstable support environments. Ultimately, the paper argues that adolescent digital mental health systems must become not only more technologically advanced, but also more behaviorally meaningful, developmentally responsive, and socially aware.

title: Fundamental Fears in Bipolar Disorder: A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis
description: Anxiety is highly prevalent in bipolar disorder, yet there is a gap in research on the underlying cognitive and emotional factors that might be influential in the development of this comorbidity. Fundamental fears are thought to underlie a range of anxiety disorders, and this systematic review and meta-analysis explores their role in bipolar disorder. The fundamental fears included were anxiety sensitivity, fear of negative evaluation, injury/illness sensitivity, fear of death, fear of pain and fear of the unknown. Four databases were searched (MEDLINE, PsychINFO, CINAHL and Web of Science) and 22 studies were identified. The majority of papers were on fear of negative evaluation, and a sub-category was created for rejection sensitivity which represented the greatest number of studies. Meta-analyses were conducted when three or more papers compared bipolar disorder participants to another condition or to controls. Included papers showed that (1) rejection sensitivity is raised in bipolar disorder compared to unipolar depression; (2) fear of negative evaluation is raised in comparison to controls but not unipolar depression and; (3) anxiety sensitivity is not raised in bipolar disorder compared to unipolar depression, although conclusions are limited by the number of papers. There was evidence of a possible relationship between fear of the unknown and bipolar disorder, but further research is required. The fundamental fears identified here may help explain the comorbidity with anxiety disorders and provide a target for future interventions.

title: Biased and Inattentive Responding Drive Apparent Metacognitive Biases in Mental Health
description: Large-scale online studies with healthy adults have documented consistent associations between transdiagnostic psychiatric traits and metacognitive biases. Here, analysis of existing and new large-scale datasets reveals that such correlations are largely driven by surface-level dimensions of questionnaire-filling behaviour: systematic rating biases and inattentive responding. Specifically, a bias to report positive or negative values in self-report scales generalizes to confidence ratings, producing spurious correlations between the two. Additionally, systematic over-confidence among inattentive responders produces spurious positive correlations between confidence and the endorsement of rare symptoms. We show that previously identified transdiagnostic dimensions of “anxiety-depression” and “compulsivity and intrusive thought,” both shown to correlate with decision confidence, map neatly onto these two biases of questionnaire-filling behaviour. In a pre-registered experiment, we further show that decision confidence and self-reported obsessive-compulsive tendencies are correlated with independent measures of inattentive and biased responding. Taken together, we find an alarming degree of influence of inattentive and biased responding over both self-report psychiatric measures and confidence ratings. When not accounted for, these factors produce a mirage of apparent metacognitive alterations in mental health. We discuss concrete precautionary measures that are needed to control for these biases.

title: The Cost of Belonging—and Leaving:  Structure, Predictors, and Mental Health Outcomes of Costly Religious Exits
description: Leaving a high-demand religion is often psychologically costly, yet most research focuses on simple outcomes rather than the structure and mechanisms of costly exit experiences. This study examined mental health outcomes associated with high-cost religious exits. Participants (N = 1221) had left the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints (LDS; n = 426), ultra-Orthodox Judaism (n = 292), fundamentalist Evangelical Christian (n = 279), and moderate/liberal Christian traditions (n = 209). Using a dimensional-categorical spectrum approach, results supported a single dimension of costly experiences composed of summed costs of leaving, negative exit experiences, spiritual harms and abuses, gender discrimination, religious/spiritual struggles, and demonic spiritual struggles. Higher costliness was predicted by religion of origin, gender, and sexual orientation. More intense costly experiences were associated with both higher PTSD symptoms and greater posttraumatic growth (PTG). Religious background moderated both outcomes: costly experiences predicted the highest PTSD among ultra-Orthodox Jewish individuals and was also elevated among LDS and fundamentalist evangelical participants, while ultra-Orthodox Jewish and fundamentalist evangelical participants reported less growth from their costly experiences. Gender moderated the relationship between costly experiences and PTG but not PTSD, with women experiencing less growth from their costly experiences. Sexual minority status moderated the relationship between costly experiences and PTSD, but not PTG. Overall, results suggest that the costly experiences associated with deidentification from high-demand religions begin not at exit, but during membership, and are strongly linked to both PTSD symptoms and PTG — with demographic moderators.

title: Comparison of informational and experiential interventions for VR acceptance in rural older adults: a feasibility study
description:
Background. Virtual reality (VR) offers a promising solution to deliver portable, engaging rehabilitation services, particularly for rural populations with limited access to care. However, its adoption among older adults may be hindered by key barriers, including technological unfamiliarity or concerns about visually induced motion sickness (VIMS). Overcoming these initial acceptance barriers is a critical step for implementing this gerontechnology which could deliver physical and mental health support directly to the homes of older adults. 

Research aim. We aimed to determine the feasibility of using brief, low-resource interventions, either an informational handout or a short immersive VR experience, to improve attitudes toward VR in rural older adults. 

Methods. In this comparative feasibility study, sixty-four rural adults aged 60 and older received either an informational handout describing VR or completed four immersive VR activities using hand tracking on a consumer headset. Attitudes toward VR and VIMS symptoms were assessed using pre-post intervention surveys.

Results. The immersive VR experience did not result in a significant increase in VIMS symptoms, demonstrating high tolerability. Both the informational handout group and the VR experience group showed significant positive improvements in attitudes toward VR.

Conclusions. Brief, low-resource interventions can increase technology acceptance for VR among rural older adults. The finding that a simple informational handout can be as effective as a hands-on immersive experience has significant, practical implications for the scalable and cost-effective deployment of VR-based technologies in clinical and home-based gerontological settings.

title: Anxious attachment increases singlehood among men, avoidant attachment increases singlehood among women
description: Rates of singlehood has risen, and it has been proposed that attachment insecurity may contribute to individuals remaining single. However, existing research has not examined whether attachment insecurity actually is associated with prolonged singlehood, nor considered whether the effects may differ by gender. The present study therefore examined whether attachment anxiety and avoidance were associated with the proportion of individuals’ lives spent in relationships versus single. Using a representative Norwegian sample of 1,390 individuals (ages 18–87, 52% women), participants reported the number of years they had spent single, in uncommitted relationships, and in long-term committed relationships—together with a diverse set of romantic–sexual experiences when single. Results indicated that attachment anxiety was associated with increased singlehood among men, whereas attachment avoidance was more strongly associated with increased singlehood among women. Attachment anxiety also increased men’s reports of being single due to attraction difficulties. Furthermore, while attachment anxiety also decreased men’s number of sexual partners, attachment anxiety increased the number of sexual partners for women. However, with increasing attachment anxiety women also reported more often feeling sexually used. The findings indicate that attachment insecurity may contribute to increases in singlehood, but should be considered in relation to gender.

title: The Truly Horrific Face of Masculinity: Unravelling the Phenomenon of a Global Online Rape Academy
description: This review elucidates the phenomenon of a global online rape academy through the lens of the psychology of men and masculinities. Triggered by recent investigative reports documenting online communities in which men exchanged strategies for sedating, sexually assaulting, recording, and distributing abuse against unconscious women, the article aims to move beyond explanations focused solely on individual pathology and instead explore broader psychosocial, cultural, and technological mechanisms that may contribute to such violence. From the outset of the Confluence Model of Sexual Aggression and drawing on the Gender Role Strain Paradigm (GRSP) and Precarious Manhood Theory (PMT), the article discusses how rigid masculinity norms emphasizing dominance, emotional restriction, entitlement, sexual conquest, and control over women may contribute to the normalization and reinforcement of misogynistic violence within digitally connected peer environments. Additional concepts, including masculine sexual entitlement, narcissistic entitlement, externalizing forms of male distress, as well as technology acceptance frameworks, are integrated to illustrate how online platforms can facilitate anonymity, group validation, tactical coordination, and the amplification of violent masculine performances. The article further highlights important explanatory aspects differing from the Confluence Model of Sexual Aggression and argues that these online networks represent not merely isolated deviance, but socially reinforced ecosystems in which violence becomes normalized, rewarded, and collectively organized. At the same time, the paper emphasizes that masculinity itself is not inherently violent and that the overwhelming majority of men do not engage in sexual violence. title: ‘Sustainable Choices’ - An Intervention to Promote Climate Change Mitigation Behaviours: A Randomized Controlled Trial
description:
Background: Individual climate change mitigation behaviours (CCMBs) can meaningfully reduce greenhouse gas emissions, yet many people report uncertainty about what actions to take and difficulty changing established habits. Scalable, digital behavioural interventions remain largely untested. This randomized controlled trial evaluated the effectiveness and acceptability of Sustainable Choices, a five-week, internet-delivered intervention designed to promote CCMBs and psychological well-being.

Methods: Adults in Sweden (N = 694) were randomized 1:1 to Sustainable Choices or a waitlist control. The primary outcome was CCMBs at post-intervention, assessed with the Climate Mitigation Behaviour Scale (CLIMBS) and analysed using item-response-theory–derived latent scores in mixed-effects models under an intention-to-treat framework. Secondary outcomes included well-being (SWEMWBS), climate-related worry (GAD-2), low mood (PHQ-2), and meaning and purpose (PROMIS-6a). Follow-ups were conducted at 1, 3, and 6 months. Complier Average Causal Effect analyses examined dose–response relations, and acceptability was assessed through adherence and satisfaction.

Results: Compared with controls, the intervention produced significantly greater increases in CCMBs on the CLIMBS general factor (d = 0.34, p < .001), with improvements in food, consumption, and engagement domains but not mobility. Meaning and purpose increased relative to controls (d = 0.23, p = .004), whereas changes in well-being, worry, and low mood were not significant. Engagement showed robust dose-dependent effects: each completed module increased CCMBs by 0.09 points, and full adherence yielded a 0.45-point gain. Satisfaction was high, with 84% recommending the course.

title: Midfrontal theta power relates to response speeding following frustrative nonreward
description: Objectives: Irritability is a transdiagnostic symptom proposed to be characterized by maladaptive responses to frustrative nonreward (FNR), including heightened negative affect (i.e., frustration). Although FNR typically elicits adaptive behavioral adjustments, the neural mechanisms that support these adjustments and their trial-by-trial dynamics remain unexplored. Midfrontal theta power (MFθ), a key marker of expectancy violation and cognitive control, is a strong candidate for indexing these mechanisms and their role in supporting adaptive responses. We investigated how fluctuations in MFθ during FNR relate to subsequent behavioral adjustments and whether these associations are moderated by individual differences in irritability and state frustration. Methods: Young adults (N = 91) completed a validated frustration paradigm and self-reported their irritability and state frustration. A multivariate approach was used to enhance the signal-to-noise ratio of single-trial MFθ. Linear mixed-effects models tested whether trial-by-trial MFθ and feedback type (win vs. FNR) predicted reaction time on the following trial. Results: Higher MFθ following FNR feedback, but not win feedback, was associated with faster reaction times on the next trial, suggesting that theta oscillations support adaptive behavioral adjustments to unexpected reward loss. Reduced MFθ to FNR feedback was linked to greater self-reported frustration, while trait irritability and state frustration did not moderate the MFθ-behavior association. Conclusion: MFθ increased following FNR feedback and predicted faster subsequent responses, highlighting its role in adaptive adjustment to frustrative outcomes. These findings enhance understanding of the neurocognitive mechanisms supporting coping with frustration and suggest this process may be less effective under heightened subjective frustration.

title: Associations Between Familial Factors and Emotion Regulation Among Preadolescents with Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder: An ABCD Study®
description: Background: Previous work has identified associations between maladaptive familial factors and risk for emotion regulation (ER) challenges among youth. Youth with attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder (ADHD) have been found to be particularly susceptible to ER challenges. Preadolescence is a key period during which changes in ER emerge, yet it remains understudied with respect to factors that impact ER among youth with ADHD, specifically. Methods: The current study leveraged Morris and colleagues’ (2007) tripartite model of parental influence on child ER to examine the salience of familial factors (i.e., parent ER, parental warmth, family conflict) on child ER as assessed via the Child Behavior Checklist Dysregulation Profile. Participants were 953 youth who met ADHD diagnostic criteria and their counterparts with fewer than four total ADHD symptoms (N=4,371) who completed the baseline visit of the Adolescent Brain Cognitive Development StudySM. Results: Youth with ADHD experienced lower ER compared to peers, consistent with extant literature. Across all youth, parent-reported family conflict was associated with lower child ER, while parental warmth was associated with greater child ER. Lower parent ER conferred the greatest risk for lower child ER, generally, and particularly among youth with ADHD. Significant associations between specific familial factors, ADHD, and subdomains of youth ER (i.e., anxious/depressed, attention, and aggression) were also identified. Conclusions: Results of the current study may offer guidance for prioritization of targets for universal prevention and family-focused ER-based interventions for youth with ADHD. Future studies should examine the effect of familial factors on youth ER throughout the transition to adolescence.

title: Adverse Mental Health Effects of Social and Emotional Learning
description: All education programs have the potential to, and likely do, cause unintended adverse effects. Using meta-analytic data, we explore the heterogeneity of mental health effects of school-based SEL programs. We report 43.1% of the 58 studies with mental health outcomes reported at least one effect opposite the intended direction. Percentages varied by study-level factors, including racial composition, implementation, and program type, with mental health and mindfulness-focused programs showing the highest adverse effects. Across 184 mental health Hedges’ g effect sizes, reflecting 14,464 students, 21% were negative for SEL. The estimated adverse effect size was -0.158 and not statistically significant compared to 0.209, which was statistically significant for beneficial effects. Sensitivity analyses indicate that the externalizing adverse effect estimate is unstable, such that removing a single study reduces the negative effect from -0.208 to -0.065. In contrast, the internalizing adverse estimate (-0.097) and positive internalizing (0.215) and positive externalizing (0.211) effects were consistent across studies. We conclude that the prevalence of adverse effects is high, and the magnitude of these effects is small to modest, with most effects clustering near zero. When considering all studies, the externalizing adverse effect is too unstable to judge with confidence and contributes to the instability of the overall estimate of the mental health adverse effect. Removing the most influential study stabilizes and substantially reduces this estimate. We discuss potential causes of adverse effects and future research directions.

title: Of Breathing and Lying:  The (Null) Effect of a Brief Mindfulness Meditation on Immoral Behavior at Work
description: Mindfulness practices have been linked to enhanced emotional regulation, cognitive control and, consequently, prosocial behavior. However, these regulatory capacities may also facilitate coping with guilt and stress following immoral actions. The present research tested whether a brief mindfulness meditation facilitates more successful lying about a bullying incident at work. In this experiment, 250 participants were randomly assigned to one of three mental exercise conditions (mindfulness, mind-wandering, positive affirmation). In a workplace-bullying cover-up paradigm, participants delivered either a false or a true statement in response to an accusation of having bullied a colleague at work. Participants who bullied a colleague and then lied about it reported significantly higher feelings of guilt and stress compared to those who told the truth about not bullying. However, this effect was not significantly moderated by mental exercise. In a follow-up study, 171 independent observers viewed the recorded statements and judged their veracity. As expected, observers were more likely to judge true statements as true compared to false statements (i.e., a stronger truth bias when judging true statements). Again, however, this effect was not significantly moderated by mental exercise. These findings suggest limited effects of brief mindfulness meditations on internal regulation and on advantages in lying.

title: Developmental Constraints on Learning and Liking Music
description:
Pleasure from sensory experience is thought to arise from the interplay between learned expectations and incoming stimuli, yet how this relationship develops across the lifespan is poorly understood. Lifetime exposure to culturally familiar stimuli confounds maturational differences in learning with differences in prior knowledge. We circumvent this problem by exposing children (5-12 years), adolescents (13-17 years), and young adults (19-24 years; total n = 237) to the Bohlen-Pierce scale, a musical system with no cultural tradition, and we manipulate exposure within a single session. All age groups formed expectations proportional to exposure, but only adolescents and adults were sensitive to structural violations in both familiarity judgments and aesthetic preference. While adults’ preference tracked exposure consistent with predictive coding accounts of reward, children preferences declined with repeated exposure.
The coupling between structural learning and hedonic experience increased across development, providing causal developmental evidence that pleasure from structured sensory input is constrained by the maturation of statistical learning.

title: My pay beats his: Attachment anxiety increases yearly salary via intrasexual competition
description:
Attachment anxiety increases status striving, driven by greater competitiveness with same-sex peers (Gasiorowska et al., 2026). It is currently unknown, however, whether anxiously attached individuals’
greater status strivings actually result in greater status attainment. Demonstrating such would highlight a previously unconsidered fitness function of attachment anxiety. The present study therefore examined
whether attachment styles predict two foundational markers of status attainment—yearly salary and educational attainment—in a representative sample of the Norwegian population (collected in 2023,
N = 1,390, Mage = 44). Results showed a $1,423 increase in yearly salary per increase in attachment anxiety via intrasexual competition. In comparison, avoidant attachment yielded only a $541 yearly increase. However, the direct association between attachment anxiety and salary was negative ($5,193), producing a net yearly salary loss of $3,769 per increase in attachment anxiety. The eventual effect of attachment anxiety on attained status may depend on whether attachment anxiety primarily channels into same-sex combativeness or partner preoccupation.

title: Other-focused goals elicit more high-engagement strategies and less expressive suppression than self-focused goals when regulating others’ emotions
description: When regulating someone’s emotions, your goal might be to make them feel better (other-focused regulation goal) or to make yourself feel better (self-focused regulation goal; e.g., reducing their distress to relieve your own negative feelings). These contrasting goals may drive differences in the regulation strategies you choose. The current pre-registered study (N = 55) uses a repeated-measures within-subjects design to compare strategies for pro-hedonic other-focused versus self-focused goals. Strategies represented low (expressive suppression, downward social comparison), moderate (humour, distraction, direct action) or high (valuing, cognitive reframing, receptive listening) engagement with the other person. Compared to self-focused goals, other-focused goals led to significantly higher valuing and listening but lower suppression. Moreover, there were significant main effects for engagement (across goals, people used more high-engagement strategies than suppression—the lowest-engagement strategy), for goals (across strategies, people engaged in greater regulation for other- than self-focused goals) and their interaction (greater use of high-engagement strategies than suppression was stronger for other- than self-focused goals). Our findings suggest that affective engagement is the primary driver of which strategies are chosen to make someone else versus yourself feel better. Future research could examine instrumental as well as hedonic goals and consider more objective assessments.

title: Using Experience Sampling Methods to Study Identity Dynamics: A 5-Step Guide
description: A dynamic perspective on identity is essential for explaining how identities emerge, stabilize, and change across everyday situations. Mounting theory and evidence show that identity varies meaningfully from moment to moment. Experience sampling methods (ESM), a data collection method where participants repeatedly provide researchers with information about their current or recent thoughts, behaviors, feelings, and contexts as they happen in real-time, is facilitating identification and documentation of intraindividual identity dynamics and the interindividual differences in those dynamics. This paper provides a five-step practical guide to ESM – full flow from theoretical specification to study design, data collection, data analysis, and results presentation and interpretation – that may be helpful for identity scholars seeking to integrate ESM in their work. In presenting each step we outline the core goals and decisions involved and provide an illustrative example, describing how specific design decisions were made in a small empirical study of how ethnic-racial and gender identity change across social situations, and how the resulting specifics and empirical results might be reported in a journal manuscript. Together with accompanying R code implementations, this guide expands identity researchers’ toolbox and the exploration and study of intraindividual identity dynamics.

title: A bad apple may not spoil the barrel: Mechanisms of trust formation under  misinformation exposure
description:
Under widespread misinformation, deciding which news sources to trust is consequential. 
Here, we examine the mechanisms people use to form trust in news sources. Across 8 
experiments, participants continuously evaluated a sequence of news posts that included one 
piece of misinformation. Then, they indicated trust in the source. For neutral content 
(Experiments 1-5), trust tracked the average reliability of the reports, whether the source was 
a news channel (Experiments 1-3) or an individual (Experiments 4-5). Despite clear detection 
of misinformation, there was no evidence for a “one strike and you’re out” mechanism. In 
contrast, for politically charged content (Experiments 6-7), Republicans continued to rely on 
averaging, whereas Democrats shifted to a mechanism that heavily penalized misinformation, 
differences that we discuss further. These findings suggest that, for neutral content, trust 
judgments follow equal-weighting strategy, but political priors can shape not only belief in 
specific reports, but the process of trusting news.

title: Measuring Cybersickness in Virtual Reality: Refinement and Validation of the Simulator Sickness Questionnaire
description:
Objective
The Simulator Sickness Questionnaire (SSQ) is widely used to assess cybersickness, but its structure and scoring may not fully reflect symptom patterns experienced in modern virtual reality (VR). This study evaluated whether a simpler restructured version could provide a more streamlined and interpretable measure while preserving its association with behavioral tolerance.

Background
Cybersickness includes symptoms such as nausea, disorientation, and eyestrain. Existing SSQ scoring uses overlapping subscales, potentially redundant items, and weighted scores that may reduce interpretability.

Method
Study 1 (N = 361) used exploratory factor analysis (EFA) on 16 SSQ items administered following VR exposure. Study 2 (N = 481) used confirmatory factor analysis (CFA) in an independent sample to compare competing models. Criterion-related validity was evaluated using behavioral tolerance measures (time in VR and early withdrawal).

Results
EFA supported a three-factor structure (strain, dizziness/disorientation, nausea). Removing weak and redundant items produced an 11-item model (VR-SSQ). CFA indicated acceptable fit, comparable to the original SSQ and alternative scoring methods. The VR-SSQ uses non-overlapping subscales scored as simple item means. All measures were strongly associated with reduced behavioral tolerance to VR (shorter exposure duration and increased likelihood of withdrawal).

Conclusion
Cybersickness reflects a multidimensional construct with a strong general component. The VR-SSQ is a reduced item set that captures this structure while retaining comparable associations with behavioral tolerance, supporting a simpler and more interpretable measurement tool.

Application
The streamlined VR-SSQ facilitates more interpretable assessment of cybersickness symptoms while reducing time to administer and scoring complexity in research and applied VR settings.

title: Metacognitive Confidence, AI Familiarity, and Heuristic Judgment in AI-Generated Text Attribution: An Exploratory Study Among Undergraduate Students
description:
Artificial intelligence (AI) systems are increasingly integrated into educational and everyday contexts, raising important questions about how individuals evaluate AI-generated content. This study examined the relationships between self-reported AI familiarity, metacognitive confidence, and judgment performance in AI-generated text attribution among undergraduate students. An exploratory cross-sectional design was employed with 66 participants who completed a forced-choice sentence judgment task consisting of 20 items, all generated using ChatGPT. After each item, participants also reported their confidence in their judgments, and self-reported AI familiarity was assessed using a Likert-type scale.
Results indicated that judgment performance was relatively low (M = .43, SD = .15), while metacognitive confidence was comparatively high (M = 3.84, SD = .87). Correlation analyses revealed a weak negative relationship between AI familiarity and judgment performance, a moderate positive relationship between AI familiarity and confidence, and a weak negative relationship between confidence and judgment performance. These findings suggest a dissociation between subjective confidence and actual performance in AI-text attribution tasks. Qualitative responses further indicated that participants frequently relied on heuristic cues, particularly perceived formality and linguistic style, when evaluating text. Overall, the findings suggest that perceived familiarity with AI systems is more strongly associated with increased confidence than with improved evaluative performance. The study contributes to emerging literature on AI literacy and metacognition by highlighting limitations in judgment calibration and the role of heuristic processing in AI-generated text evaluation.

title: Growing Together or Growing Apart: How Peer Interaction Shapes Children’s Mental Health After COVID-19
description: The COVID-19 pandemic substantially altered children’s opportunities for peer interaction, yet little is known about how early post-pandemic peer interactions relate to subsequent socioemotional development. Using data from 1,057 children in the National Project on Achievement in Twins (NatPAT), the present study examined whether parent-reported peer interactions in Fall 2021 predicted trajectories of emotional and behavioural difficulties (SDQ Total Difficulties; TD) and prosocial behaviour (PR) from 2021 to 2023. Linear latent growth curve models with fixed time scores were estimated using robust maximum likelihood, accounting for clustering at the family level. Across both outcomes, children showed modest average change over time, with substantial individual differences in baseline levels. Peer interaction variables were more consistently associated with initial socioemotional adjustment than with rates of change. Higher peer conflict predicted greater initial TD and lower initial PR, whereas having more close friends was associated with fewer TD at baseline. Peer predictors explained statistically non-significant variance in growth slopes, suggesting limited influence on individual differences in post-pandemic socioemotional trajectories. These findings indicate that children’s early post-pandemic peer environments were informative for understanding initial socioemotional status but contributed little to explaining subsequent change.

title: Measuring children’s motivation for music: a systematic review of quantitative research tools.
description: Motivation for engaging with music is considered a critical aspect of child musicality and has significant implications for development. Despite this there is a notable lack of research into motivation for music during childhood, likely because motivation is a complex and multifaceted construct which is difficult to measure. The current research aimed to facilitate further research into this underexplored area by (1) uncovering existing approaches to assessing children’s motivation for musical engagement and (2) developing a new open-access database to assist researchers in finding appropriate measures for future studies. A systematic review of papers published before April 2023 that report the quantitative assessment of children’s motivation for music (0- to 11-years-old) was conducted. Seventy-nine unique scales were identified. Details on scale design, psychometrics and samples were catalogued in a new database: ‘Measuring Motivation for Music’. An analysis of the database examined whether the identified tools were (1) psychometrically robust, (2) suitable for measuring motivation for music in young and neurodiverse populations and (3) able to account for the wide variety of musical activities available to children. Our results indicated that existing scales were mostly valid and reliable self-report questionnaires designed for older (6+ years) neurotypical children that assessed intrinsic motivation for playing an instrument. Going forwards, assessments should additionally investigate extrinsic motivation, incorporate a wider range of musical activities, use simpler language to cater for younger groups and those with language difficulties.

title: The impact of hybrid working on stress: An Ecological Momentary Assessment study of stress dynamics and variation across the day and by type of day
description:
Objectives: COVID-19 accelerated a transformational change in working practices, with large numbers of employees now combining working from home (WFH) with working from elsewhere (WFE) in a hybrid work pattern.  How hybrid working influences stress is not yet well understood.  The aim of this study was to utilise Ecological Momentary Assessment (EMA) to examine how real-time perceived stress dynamics differed across the day by work arrangement (work vs non-work; WFH vs WFE).   

Design: Single wave of EMA intensive longitudinal assessment

Method: Twenty-two (female n=16) desk-based hybrid working university employees were recruited.  Using the EMA RealLife Exp App, participants received notifications to respond to two perceived stress question five times per day at random intervals for up to 21 days, and reported work arrangement at the end of the day.   Data were analysed using two-level dynamic structural equation modelling (DSEM) in Mplus 8.11 .

Results: In total 1818 EMA prompts were delivered, of which 1386 were completed, with mean compliance 74.9%.  Participants worked on average 9.68 (SD=3.77) days, spending 4.18 (SD=2.67) days WFH, and 5.5 days WFE (SD=3.02).  Stress during 15:00-17:59 was significantly lower on non-working days compared to working days (β = -0.130, 95% CI [-0.255, -0.004].  WFH showed greater midday stress between 12:00-14:59 (β = 0.396, 95% CI [0.207, 0.559]) and higher evening stress between 18:00-20:59 (β = 0.207, 95% CI [0.020, 0.391]. 

Conclusion: Work arrangements impact stress differentially across the day, with stress elevated during WFH at specific ‘pinch’ points during the day compared with WFE.

title: The Problem of Common False-Alarm Rates and the Informational Asymmetry When Comparing Pure and Mixed Lists in Recognition Memory:  Reconsidering the List-Strength Effect
description: The list-strength effect (LSE)—the interaction between item strength and list composition (pure versus mixed)—is theoretically diagnostic in models of memory. In contrast to free recall, in old-new recognition, the LSE was long considered negligible. This dissociation prompted the development of new recognition models. Recent work, however, suggests that the magnitude and direction of the LSE depend on the strength manipulation. Here, we argue that conclusions about the LSE are undermined by two methodological limitations in pure-mixed comparisons: a design flaw and an informational asymmetry. Sensitivity measures in recognition memory depend jointly on hit and false-alarm rates (HRs and FARs), which co-vary when sensitivity, response bias, or both change. When strength conditions differ only for studied items, sensitivity estimates from pure and mixed lists are not constructed from equivalent components. This is because traditional mixed-list designs, which impose a common FAR across strength conditions, are compared to pure lists wherein FARs can vary freely. Critically, there is no contingency in which given differences in HRs, a common FAR of any magnitude would lead researchers to attribute those differences to bias rather than to sensitivity—regardless of which sensitivity measure is used. We consider two possible arguments in favor of common FARs and refute both. Using a hypothetical reanalysis of recent LSE data, we show that empirically plausible changes in FAR—without altering observed HRs—can produce LSEs of any direction. We conclude that pure-mixed comparisons cannot adjudicate between theories of recognition memory. Alternative experimental designs are then discussed.

title: Developmental Differences in Prefrontal Dynamics During Motor Sequence Learning
description: Acquiring a new motor skill recruits the prefrontal cortex (PFC) for cognitive control, and this engagement is dynamically modulated as proficiency develops. Although practice-related changes in PFC activation are well documented in adults, how children modulate PFC engagement during learning and whether individual differences in executive function (EF) shape this process remain poorly understood. We measured PFC activation using fNIRS while children (6–9 years) and young adults (18–25 years) learned a short piano sequence over 30 minutes of practice. Both groups reached comparable asymptotic accuracy, but adults learned at a significantly faster rate even though the task was deliberately simplified for children. Adults showed an inverted-U trajectory of left prefrontal activation, and the steepness of the early rise was positively correlated with individual learning rate, providing a neural signature of efficient dynamic modulation. Children, by contrast, engaged right vlPFC channels at a sustained level throughout practice with no evidence of dynamic modulation. A shared decline at the right frontal pole was observed in both groups and was moderated by initial accuracy, which was in turn predicted by EF. These findings suggest that efficient motor skill acquisition in adults is supported by the rapid engagement and subsequent withdrawal of prefrontal resources, whereas children remain engaged with the task throughout practice even when task demands are well within their capacity, pointing to developmental differences in the flexibility of prefrontal modulation during motor learning.

title: Outcome Versus Process Focused Future Thinking: Results from a Randomised Experiment
description: Future thinking plays a central role in emotion and behaviour, yet different modes of simulation may have distinct effects. This pre-registered experiment compared outcome- and process-focused future thinking on affective and cognitive responses to imagined events. It was hypothesised that anticipated pleasure, anticipatory pleasure and positive affect would be higher in an outcome-focused task relative to a process-focused task. Further, ratings of perceived control and likelihood of the future event will be higher after a process-focused task relative to the outcome-focused. Participants (N = 134; M age = 35.1 years, SD = 13.1) generated personally relevant future events and were randomly assigned to focus on either outcomes or the steps required to achieve them. Outcome-focused thinking increased anticipatory pleasure, motivation, and personal significance. In contrast, process-focused thinking reduced perceived control and was associated with reductions in both anticipated and anticipatory pleasure. No effects were observed for perceived likelihood, and positive affect increased modestly across conditions. These findings indicate that outcome-focused future thinking enhances affective engagement, whereas process-focused thinking may introduce constraints that attenuate perceived control and reward-related responses. Distinguishing between these modes of future thinking has implications for models of motivation and interventions targeting future-oriented cognition.

title: Rhythm Abstraction in Bumble Bees Remains Inconclusive
description: Zeng et al. (2026) report rhythm abstraction in bumble bees. While we applaud this effort to expand the examination of rhythm perception into the insect clade, we argue that the evidence for rhythmic generalization remains inconclusive. The stimuli used to test tempo-invariance were not proportional transformations, as inter-flash gaps remained fixed across conditions. Discrimination in Experiment 3 could be explained by simpler local perceptual cues or absolute duration matching rather than global rhythmic patterns. The claim that “bumble bees also form robust abstract rhythm representations” is thus not supported by the study.

title: Determinants of Participation and Support Mechanisms in a Paralympic Sport Training Program: Evidence from the IDRD Program in Bogotá
description: Background: While Paralympic sport programs are increasingly recognized for their contribution to the well-being and social inclusion of people with disabilities, less attention has been given to the factors that facilitate or constrain athletes’ participation within these programs. Understanding how individual motivation, support systems, and structural barriers influence engagement in sport programs is particularly relevant in under-researched contexts such as Latin America. This study aims to: a) describe the socio-demographic and sport participation profiles of athletes involved in a Paralympic sport training program in Bogotá, Colombia; b) examine the role of support systems—such as coaches, family members, and teammates—in shaping athletes’ engagement in the program; and c) identify key motivations and barriers influencing sustained participation in Paralympic sport. Methods: A quantitative research design was used to collect data from athletes participating in the Paralympic sport training program implemented by the Instituto Distrital de Recreación y Deporte (IDRD) in Bogotá, Colombia. Data were gathered through a structured questionnaire examining athletes’ demographic characteristics, sport participation history, sources of support, motivations for engagement in sport, and perceived barriers to participation. Descriptive and exploratory analyses were conducted to examine patterns of participation and program-related factors. Results: Results indicate that athletes’ engagement in the program is strongly supported by multiple social actors, particularly coaches, family members, and teammates. Coaching support emerged as a key enabling factor, with athletes reporting that encouragement and confidence expressed by coaches played an important role in sustaining their motivation. Family support also contributed significantly to continued participation. Athletes reported motivations related to improving physical well-being, enhancing appearance, and achieving spo

title: A meta-analytic database of 789 choice architecture interventions from 280 experiments coded on 298 variables
description: The impact of choice architecture interventions—psychologically-informed changes to communications, layouts, and processes—is context dependent. How well a given intervention works to nudge a given behavior depends on who is being nudged, where, when, by whom, and to do what. In order to help researchers explore the context-dependency of interventions, we built a database of 789 interventions from 280 randomized controlled experiments published between 2018 and 2023 by academic and practitioner sources. We developed a custom coding infrastructure to encode 298 variables that describe the domain, geography, population, behavior, intervention techniques, and standardized effect sizes, as well as variables describing elements of the experimental design. Variables come from multiple behavioral science taxonomies and cover binary, continuous, and qualitative values. Coding followed a series of quality checks across inclusion, extraction, consensus, audit, and author review. The analysis-ready database, a digital repository of visual intervention stimuli, coding templates and processes, relevant code, and an interactive explorer are deposited as open resources. [Publicly available after peer review.]

title: Making Food VAT Reform Tangible: Concrete Price Information Increases Public Acceptance
description: Increasing the value-added tax (VAT) on animal- and reducing it on plant-based foods can reduce greenhouse gas emissions and diet-related disease burden by shifting consumption toward more sustainable dietary patterns. Yet, public acceptance remains low. Two pre-registered online experiments in Germany examined whether acceptance is linked to cost overestimation and whether communicating accurate price information increases public support. In Study 1 (N = 161), participants submitted a personal grocery receipt and were randomly assigned to one of three VAT scenarios: an increase on animal-based products (7% to 19%), a reduction on plant-based products (7% to 0%), or both. Policy acceptance was measured before and after participants estimated the price change of their receipt and received feedback on the actual change. Although participants systematically misestimated costs, initial acceptance (β = .92, p < .001) rather than misestimation (β = .03, p = .329) was the dominant predictor of subsequent acceptance. When given the opportunity to eliminate products from their receipt after receiving feedback on the actual change, participants predominantly removed meat and dairy. Study 2 (N = 299) focused on the VAT combination policy using a standardized €30 receipt. Participants either estimated costs before receiving feedback, received accurate price information only, or received only a policy description. Acceptance in the estimation (d = .54) and information (d = .33) conditions significantly increased compared to the control condition, while misestimation showed no significant relationship with acceptance. These findings suggest that expressing price changes in Euros rather than VAT percentages represents a simple, scalable strategy for increasing public support for sustainable food taxation.

title: Mind the Research Culture Gap: Staff Perspectives on Ethical, Inclusive, and Sustainable Research Practice at a UK Research Intensive University
description: Research culture reform increasingly requires researchers to attend to ethical, inclusive, and sustainable practice, yet little is known about how staff perceive the gap between what is valued and what is enacted. This mixed-methods study surveyed 244 staff at a UK research-intensive university, comparing ratings of how important each practice should be (ideal) with perceptions of how far it is currently realised (actual) across ethics, inclusion (operationalised as community-based research), and sustainability. Ratings were collected at three actor levels, the participant, their peers, and their institution. This allowed an examination of where university staff identify the largest research culture change barriers. Paired-samples t-tests revealed significant ideal-actual gaps across all domains, with sustainability showing the largest differences and ethics the smallest. A consistent self-other narrative emerged: participants rated their own practice most favourably, with the largest gaps between their own practice and that of their peers. For ethics, the individual-level gap was negligible, consistent with the procedural formalisation of ethical review. For sustainability, gaps were substantial at every level. Open-text responses contextualised these patterns, revealing that ethical practice was framed as individually controllable, while inclusion was seen as context-dependent and collectively constrained, and sustainability practice as routinely blocked by structural barriers. These findings suggest that procedural formalisation can narrow the ideal-actual gap in research culture change but may foster surface compliance rather than reflexive engagement. We conclude that the path to research culture change, particularly in respect of sustainability and inclusion, requires structural reform as well as individual behaviour change.

title: The Promise and Peril of Social Media: How Context Shapes Online Risks and Digital Literacy Among Marginalised Adolescents in a Semi-Rural South African Community
description: Debates about online risks often overlook the realities of young people navigating structural adversity and inequality. This qualitative study explores how adolescents in a low-income, semi-rural South African community navigate the double-edged nature of social media. Drawing on in-depth interviews, we show how offline violence, gendered power dynamics, and structural inequalities are entangled with online experiences, creating overlapping risks that amplify existing vulnerabilities. Simultaneously, social media is a source of entertainment, belonging, and glimpses of alternative futures, particularly for adolescents with personal smartphone access. Digital literacy in this context is informal and reactive, shaped by peers and trusted adults rather than formal education. These findings show how local contexts structure both the benefits and harms of social media as well as the forms of digital literacy that develop.

title: “It’s a Trap!” – Faking in multidimensional forced choice response formats: Latent change score modeling of faking across MFC and RS formats
description: The present study examines the faking susceptibility of rating scale (RS) and multidimensional forced-choice (MFC) questionnaires in high-stakes as opposed to low-stakes assessment contexts. Following the transformation of a situation-based Big Five questionnaire (B5PS; Ziegler, 2014) from a RS into an MFC response format and a successful Thurstonian IRT (TIRT) calibration, the MFC version was evaluated in a lab-simulated high-stakes assessment situation. The vulnerability of MFC and RS formats to intentional response distortion was assessed in a within-subject design (N = 187). Participants were instructed to assume the role of applicants in a fictitious job application process and were encouraged to fake their responses on both the MFC questionnaire and a standard RS Big Five inventory (BIF-2; Danner et al., 2016). In the faking condition, participants were asked to present themselves as ideal candidates according to a predefined job requirement profile, targeting selected Big Five domains, namely Conscientiousness, Emotional Stability, and Agreeableness. Latent Change Score Modelling (LCSM) was then applied to model faking behavior at the individual level across honest and faking conditions for both response formats. Analyses revealed a strong faking effect in the RS format, whereas the LCSM did not fit the MFC data for any Big Five domain except Agreeableness (A). Results demonstrate the reduced faking susceptibility of the MFC format relative to the RS format. A coherent faking factor did not emerge in the MFC format, while homogeneous faking behavior was evident in the RS format. These findings are discussed in relation to current empirical evidence on the susceptibility of MFC formats to faking in high-stakes assessment situations, with reference to low-stakes assessment contexts. The specific role of Emotional Stability (N) in the faking susceptibility of MFC questionnaires is highlighted, corroborating findings from previous research.

title: Temporal Dynamics of Selective Enumeration for a Small Number of Emotional Faces
description: Face-to-face communication with a small number of others requires perceiving each person’s facial expressions, as emotional states often vary across people. Although multiple-object individuation, defined as the representation of distinct entities in a scene, has been investigated for geometric figures using event-related potentials (ERPs) during enumeration tasks, the extent to which these processes apply to social entities remains largely unclear. The present study aimed to examine the temporal dynamics of selective enumeration of emotional faces in a small group context. Thirty participants viewed four faces (two per hemifield) for 200 ms and enumerated zero, one, or two happy faces in a cued target hemifield, with the remaining faces displaying neutral expressions. Behavioral results confirmed accurate target enumeration. Lateralized ERPs relative to the cued target hemifield, specifically the P1 posterior contralateral (90–150 ms poststimulus onset), N2 posterior contralateral (250–300 ms poststimulus), and contralateral delay activity (400–600 ms), were all modulated by target numerosity. These findings suggest that individuated representations of up to two happy faces were formed during early-to-intermediate processing stages and subsequently maintained in working memory. Overall, the results provide an initial step toward understanding the neurocognitive mechanisms underlying group-member individuation, which may support effective interactions in small groups.

title: Build Better Relationships: Positive Empathy and Capitalization
description: When individuals share positive events with others, they can experience benefits beyond the positive event itself, a phenomenon known as capitalization. However, the perceived quality of the responder’s reaction to a capitalization attempt shapes the impact it will have for the capitalizer. Here, we examined how different dimensions of empathy (e.g., compassion, perspective taking, emotion sharing) in listeners predict perceived responses to capitalization attempts by sharers. We recruited 103 stranger dyads (N = 206) who engaged in naturalistic conversations about a meaningful positive event. Participants watched video recordings of their interactions and continuously rated their own and their partner's emotions using a sliding scale. Results revealed that co-experienced positive affect—moments when both the listener and sharer simultaneously experienced positive emotions—was a key predictor of perceived responses to capitalization attempts. Specifically, more moments of shared positive affect predicted greater active-constructive responses (enthusiastic, supportive reactions) and fewer passive-destructive responses (disinterested, unsupportive reactions). These associations remained robust controlling for individual moments of positive and negative affect, disclosure depth, and other empathy dimensions. These findings suggest that feeling positive emotions with others, more so than understanding or caring for their emotions, is associated with effective responses to capitalization attempts. This research bridges empathy and capitalization literatures by demonstrating that positive emotion sharing underpins supportive responses to shared good news, with important implications for understanding how to build stronger relationships through effective responses to others' positive experiences.

title: Causal judgments in complex situations
description: The Counterfactual Simulation Model (CSM) proposes that people make causal judgments by mentally simulating what would have happened in relevant counterfactual scenarios. The model assumes causal judgments incorporate two aspects: whether-causation (would the outcome have occurred without the candidate cause?) and how-causation (did the candidate cause affect how the outcome occurred?). The CSM successfully predicts judgments in simple billiard ball scenarios (2 or 3 balls). Here, we explore whether it captures people's judgments in more complex situations (up to 12 balls). We measured whether-causation (Experiment 1), how-causation (Experiment 2), and causal judgments (Experiment 3) for billiard ball scenarios varying in complexity (2-12 balls). A model combining both whether- and how-causation best predicted causal judgments, though a how-causation only model performed almost as well. However, the CSM's whether-causation predictions diverged from human judgments in complex scenarios, while how-causation predictions remained robust. This suggests that when participants make causal judgments, they might shift from counterfactual simulation toward simpler force-tracking heuristics as complexity increases.

title: A Sensory-Origin Model of Prospective Timing
description: Prospective timing, the ability to judge the duration of ongoing events, is critical for everyday functioning, such as coordinating actions, interpreting communication, and anticipating outcomes. While influential theories, including Scalar Expectancy Theory and the Striatal Beat Frequency model, have shaped our understanding of timing, they leave unresolved how the timing process is first triggered. This article proposes the Sensory-Origin Timing (SOT) model, a novel mechanism whereby prospective timing is initiated by sensory organs, with their activity providing the source for duration estimation. Specifically, we suggest that the total activity generated by the sensory organ during the transduction of a stimulus is directly related to its duration and is monitored by the striatum to form a neural representation of elapsed time. Two electroretinography studies tested this proposal in the visual modality. In Study 1, retinal activity predicted subjective duration judgments even when objective stimulus duration was held constant. In Study 2, retinal activity conformed to two fundamental scalar principles of prospective timing: mean accuracy and Weber’s law. These findings are consistent with the SOT model, providing direct support for its validity. By grounding the origin of duration perception in sensory activity, SOT addresses key limitations of existing cognitive and neurobiological theories, provides a bridge between them, and delivers a unified framework that can explain established temporal distortions and cross-modal differences. More broadly, by clarifying how timing is initiated, SOT strengthens the theoretical foundations of time perception and advances our understanding of its role in cognition and behaviour.

title: Supporting Bystander Intervention Through Conversational AI: Experimental Evidence from Undergraduate Samples
description: Bystanders play a critical role in supporting victims in situations of harm. Across campuses and workplaces, bystander intervention training aids individuals in developing effective intervention strategies. However, people’s reluctance to practice and intervene when needed remains a persistent challenge. One potential solution is to provide a safe, judgment-free space where people can repeatedly practice skills and receive personalized feedback. Here we test a chatbot-based bystander intervention practice tool, where an AI agent guides users through evidence-based training. Across two experiments with undergraduates, one conducted on a local college campus and the other online, we found that chatbot-guided training improved participants’ bystander efficacy and attitudes, with positive trends for measures of psychological safety and norm perceptions. To our knowledge, this research provides the first empirical evidence of the effectiveness of a chatbot in bystander intervention training. These findings reinforce the potential of AI as a uniquely useful pedagogical tool for promoting prosocial motivation, and, more broadly, this work contributes to efforts to cultivate safer and more inclusive social environments.

title: Extracting Semantic Representations from Word Co-occurrence Statistics: Polysemes and Homonyms
description: Vectors of word co-occurrence statistics from large corpora of natural language have previously been shown to provide good representations of lexical semantics and are now widely used resources in numerous language applications and models of human behaviour.  This paper explores the open question of how the blending of multiple word meanings associated with polysemy and homonymy affect the quality of those corpus-derived semantic representations.  Given the obvious difficulties involved in extracting the necessary information for real polysemes and homonyms, a general method is developed for evaluating the potential performance degradation by creating artificial polysemes and homonyms that can be expected to behave in the same way as their real counterparts.  It is shown that words with multiple semantically similar senses (i.e., many polysemes) do not exhibit any problems – in fact they can have improved quality semantic vectors.  However, it is confirmed that words with multiple semantically dissimilar senses (i.e., homonyms and some polysemes) can sometimes result in poorer quality semantic vectors that involve interesting interactions with the frequencies associated with the multiple senses, though often the quality degradation is less than might be anticipated.  A series of computational experiments is designed and results presented to provide clear explanations of the various issues affecting these outcomes, and to provide a thorough systematic evaluation of potential methods for improving the quality of poorly performing homonym vectors.  The general pattern of artificial homonym outcomes and the optimal method discovered for improving vector performance are then tested successfully on real homonyms.

title: What makes us think it through? Examining the relationships between feedback, confidence, and deliberation.
description: Deliberative, effortful thinking supports better reasoning about science, politics, and everyday problems, but what drives its engagement remains unclear. One possibility is that low confidence acts as a trigger for deliberation. Across four preregistered experiments (N ≈ 1,200), we provide a causal test of this hypothesis. Participants received manipulated feedback about their performance on classic reasoning problems (bat-and-ball or base-rate tasks) presented in standard, single response formats (Studies 1-2) or two-response formats in which participants give both a timed and an untimed response for each problem (Studies 3-4). In the single-response studies, negative feedback reliably reduced confidence and increased response times compared to control and positive feedback. In the two-response studies, negative feedback again reduced confidence and lengthened response times. Critically, it also increased the likelihood of revising initial answers and prolonged second-stage response times—hallmarks of deliberation. Moreover, feedback-affected confidence, measured immediately after initial, timed responses and before deliberation was possible, predicted both revisions and extended second-stage processing. Together, these findings offer robust causal evidence that confidence regulates the deployment of deliberative reasoning and clarify what makes us “think it through”.

title: Investigating Monotony in Air Traffic Control Towers: Comparing a Small and Medium-sized Airport
description:
This study investigates the development of monotony in air traffic control (ATC) using a multi-modal measurement setup applied in a field study at two operational towers of differing traffic intensity: Tartu (low-traffic) and Tallinn (medium-traffic). The results provide a first step toward establishing a reference baseline for assessing monotony in uneventful low-traffic tower environments using an evidence-based approach. Monotony is conceptualized as a state of reduced physiological and cognitive activation resulting from low task stimulation, repetitive and uneventful operational contexts. We operationalized this concept using indicators of monotony based on eye tracking to measure blink duration, PERCLOS and frequency, as well as saccade velocity. Other measures included electrocardiography (ECG), the Karolinska Sleepiness Scale (KSS), and the Psychomotor Vigilance Task (PVT). These measures were collected across multiple shifts over a period of eight days from seven air traffic controllers.
Linear mixed-effects models (LMM) were fitted to each indicator, revealing consistent time-on-task effects at Tartu across several modalities, including blink duration, percentage eye closure (PERCLOS), heart rate (HR), root mean
square of successive differences (RMSSD), and standard deviation of NN intervals (SDNN). These findings support a pattern of growing parasympathetic activation and reduced arousal associated with monotony. In contrast, Tallinn showed signs of active physiological regulation under higher workload conditions, such as elevated baseline HR and decreasing SDNN, indicative of sustained engagement. The sympathovagal balance (LF/HF) ratio increased over time at both sites, but in the context of stable or increasing RMSSD/SDNN at Tartu, this may reflect compensatory physical activity rather than sympathetic dominance. Monotony indicators differed significantly between towers, with up to a 7.0-fold stronger temporal change in PERCLOS and a 1.4-fold differenc

title: When Desire Fluctuates, So Does Radicalism: A Four-Wave Longitudinal Study of Sociosexuality, Authoritarianism, Dominance, and Sexism
description:
Reproductive interests have been proposed as an ultimate origin of ideological beliefs. In particular, individual differences in short-term mating strategies have been identified as explaining endorsement
of authoritarian, dominance-oriented, and sexist ideologies. These connections have been examined cross-sectionally and experimentally, yet no studies to date have examined whether naturalistic
